approved_users.grain: One person who may sign in. This is the authentication table: the product does not use Supabase Auth for its own users, so a row here IS an account — credential, role, tenant and profile in one.

governance.note: READ THE POLICIES BEFORE TRUSTING THIS ROW. The table carries two policies and they contradict each other: "Users can check their own login credentials" is `FOR SELECT USING (true)`, and "No direct access - use RPCs" is `FOR ALL TO authenticated, anon USING (false)`. Postgres policies are PERMISSIVE unless declared RESTRICTIVE, and permissive policies are OR'd — so the deny-all does not deny anything, and the intended rule ("no direct access") is not the enforced one. Whether that is reachable depends on the table GRANTs Supabase applies outside `supabase/migrations/`, which no static replay can see and which PLAN.md §15 is the way to settle. Recorded as D28 and assigned to WP 2.4, which owns the RESTRICTIVE-policy decision for the whole schema; it is named here because a reader of this page must not take `rls_enabled: true` for "reads are restricted".

policies.name: Users can check their own login credentials

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: The user's identity, and the value every other governance table joins on — `organization_members.user_id`, `projects.modeler_id`, the `_user_id` argument of `capabilities_for_user()` and of `get_current_user_org_id()`.

columns.name: password_hash
columns.meaning: The bcrypt hash of the account's password. A credential, and the reason the contradiction recorded in `governance.note` above is a security finding rather than an untidiness.

columns.name: role
columns.meaning: The account's global role — `admin`, `modeler`, `user` or `super_admin`. GLOBAL, not per-project and not per-organization: it is the left-most input to `capabilities_for_user()`'s role -> org -> user merge, and `super_admin` short-circuits that merge to grant everything.

substitutions.when: an account is created without an organization
substitutions.visible_as: nowhere — and that is the defect. The string is a real tenant name to every comparison that reads it, so accounts that fall to the default share one tenant with each other without any surface saying so.

columns.note: Half of D13. A displayable, editable, non-unique string used as a join key. It is kept, not dropped: `organization_id` is nullable and the rows D27 left unstamped have nothing else to authorize on. Every live comparison now goes through `org_is_current_user_org(uuid, text)`, so when §15 confirms the backfill at 100 % the text branch is removed from one function body rather than from 107 call sites.

columns.name: display_name
columns.meaning: The name the user chose for themselves, overriding `name` in the UI.

columns.name: avatar_url
columns.meaning: URL of the user's profile image, if they uploaded one.

columns.name: phone
columns.meaning: Contact number. Not used for authentication or for any second factor.

columns.name: password_changed_at
columns.meaning: When the password was last set. Server-stamped.

columns.name: password_expires_at
columns.meaning: When the current password stops being accepted — `now() + 90 days` at the time the row was written.

substitutions.value: 90 days after the row is written
substitutions.visible_as: the column default; the account pages render the resulting date

columns.name: force_password_change
columns.meaning: Whether the user must set a new password before continuing. Set when an administrator resets an account.

columns.name: is_active
columns.meaning: Whether the account may sign in. Checked at login; it is not consulted by any RLS policy, so deactivating a user does not by itself revoke a session already holding a set `app.current_user_id`.

columns.name: organization_id
columns.meaning: The user's tenant, by uuid — the same organization `organization` names, and the plane that survives a rename. What `get_current_user_org_id(_user_id)` returns.
columns.note: NULLABLE, and rows are genuinely NULL here. It was added and backfilled once by `20260709000002`; WP 2.1 re-ran the backfill matching on `name` OR `slug` and leaving ambiguous matches alone rather than picking one. A row whose text org matches no organization — `'default_org'`, or a tenant renamed and re-typed — stays NULL and keeps working on the text branch. How many is a §15 question; no work-package session can reach the database.

approved_users.note: The table WP 1.4 found existed in production but in no migration — the authentication table, untracked for a year, discovered by the orphan rule (D4). `20250815000000_approved_users_base.sql` now builds it on a fresh database, and the parts of that file which are reconstruction rather than evidence are marked as such in it. This sidecar describes the table as the migrations now define it.

audit_logs.grain: One recorded action, on one plane. `admin` is what a super admin did, `data` is a tier transition — a write to tier 2, 3 or 4 — and `access` is a governed decision such as an export being allowed or refused.

governance.note: Two SELECT policies, and they are PERMISSIVE on purpose. A super admin reads every plane; an admin of the SAME ORGANIZATION as the actor reads that org's `data` and `access` rows. They grant DISJOINT slices, so the OR that D28 makes unavoidable is the intended union here rather than an accidental escape hatch — which is worth stating, because the same shape on `approved_users` IS the defect. There is no write policy: rows arrive from SECURITY DEFINER functions and from statement-level triggers, never from a client, so RLS denying writes by default is the enforcement (WP 2.2's pattern). `audited: false` on the audit table is not a joke — nothing records reads of it, and a deletion would leave no trace. Tamper-evidence is a Phase 4 question (hash-chaining a log is the same machinery as `input-hash`), not a WP 2.3 one.

policies.name: audit: org admins read their own org's data and access rows
policies.using: plane IN ('data','access') AND EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.approved_users me JOIN public.approved_users actor ON actor.id = audit_logs.actor_user_id WHERE me.id = public.get_current_user_id() AND me.role = 'admin'::public.app_role AND me.organization_id IS NOT NULL AND me.organization_id = actor.organization_id )
policies.with_check: plane IN ('data','access') AND EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.approved_users me JOIN public.approved_users actor ON actor.id = audit_logs.actor_user_id WHERE me.id = public.get_current_user_id() AND me.role = 'admin'::public.app_role AND me.organization_id IS NOT NULL AND me.organization_id = actor.organization_id )

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: The row's identity. Returned by the emit functions so a caller can cite what it wrote.

columns.name: actor_user_id
columns.meaning: Who did it. NULLABLE, and the null carries meaning: a service-role write with no session context has no attributable actor.
columns.note: THE HONEST LIMIT OF THIS TABLE. `audit_tier_write()` reads `get_current_user_id()`, which resolves only when the caller set `app.current_user_id`. The ingest and ETL edge functions run as the service role and do not, so their rows say WHAT changed and WHEN and record `actor_known: false` in `after` rather than inventing a WHO. That is worth having and it is not attribution; closing it means those functions setting user context, which is their change to make (§16, WP 2.3).

columns.name: action
columns.meaning: What happened. Admin-plane rows use the existing dotted vocabulary (`org.update`, `api_key.revoke`); data-plane rows use the SQL operation (`insert`, `update`, `delete`); access-plane rows use `export.allowed` / `export.refused`. Three vocabularies in one column, which is a cost of one table and is recorded here rather than discovered by a reader.

columns.name: target_type
columns.meaning: What kind of thing was acted on — a table name on the data plane, an entity name on the others.

columns.name: target_id
columns.meaning: Which one, as text. NULL on data-plane rows: a statement-level trigger records a STATEMENT, and a statement that touched 5,000 rows has no single id.

columns.name: before
columns.meaning: The prior state, where the writer knows it. Admin RPCs capture it; data-plane trigger rows do NOT — a statement-level trigger has the transition tables but writing 5,000 prior rows into one jsonb would make the log unreadable and unbounded. Their row COUNT is in `after` instead.

columns.name: after
columns.meaning: The resulting state, or — on a data-plane row — the shape of the statement: `tier`, `rows_after`, `rows_before` and `actor_known`. On an access-plane row it carries the decision and what was asked for.

columns.name: ip
columns.meaning: Caller IP where the writer recorded one. Never set by the triggers, which run inside the database.

columns.name: user_agent
columns.meaning: Caller user agent where the writer recorded one. As with `ip`, absent on trigger-written rows.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When it happened. Server-stamped, and the column the plane index orders by.

columns.name: plane
columns.meaning: Which plane the action belongs to — `admin`, `data` or `access`, CHECK-constrained. Added by WP 2.3; every row that predates it is `admin` by construction, because the only writer was `log_admin_action()`, which refuses anyone who is not a super admin.

substitutions.when: a row is written without naming a plane
substitutions.visible_as: the column default, which is also what makes the `admin_audit_logs` compatibility view writable for callers that have not moved yet

audit_logs.note: Coverage on the data plane is by TRIGGER, not by instrumented RPCs, and the difference is the point. WP 2.3's gap check measured 22 live SQL functions writing tier 2/3/4 with none emitting an audit row, plus six more write paths in edge functions running as the service role. Editing the 22 would have been the obvious reading of "emit on every tier transition" and would have missed all six, and would have missed the twenty-third function somebody writes next month. A statement-level trigger on each of the twelve tier 2/3/4 tables catches every writer that exists and every writer added later.

capabilities.grain: One thing a user may or may not be permitted to do — a page they may open or a feature they may use. The CATALOG: it says what rights exist, never who holds them. The four grant tables answer that.

governance.note: Read is open — every client needs the catalog to render a permissions screen, and the rows contain no tenant data. Writes are service-role only, and in practice happen in migrations: a capability is introduced by the feature that needs it, not by an administrator at runtime.

columns.name: key
columns.meaning: The capability's identity, and the string every grant table and every call site names. Page keys are ROUTES (`/policies`); feature keys are snake_case verbs (`data_edit_inputs`). The convention is not enforced by a CHECK.

columns.name: kind
columns.meaning: `page` or `feature`, CHECK-constrained. The resolver aggregates the two separately and returns them under separate keys, so the distinction is load-bearing rather than descriptive.

columns.name: label
columns.meaning: The human name shown on permission screens.

columns.name: description
columns.meaning: One sentence on what holding it lets you do. Nullable.

columns.name: sort_order
columns.meaning: Display order on permission screens. Presentation only.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the capability was added to the catalog. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When its metadata last changed. Server-stamped.

capabilities.note: THE CATALOG IS DUPLICATED IN TYPESCRIPT. `src/lib/capabilities.ts` carries the same keys as a union type and a list, because the client needs them without a round trip. Two hand-maintained copies of one fact is an I1 violation waiting to drift — `projectMembership.test.ts` asserts the WP 2.2 keys agree, but nothing checks the whole catalog, and the honest count is that the DB has grown keys the TS list learned about only when someone noticed. Generating one from the other is the fix and it belongs with the contract's other generators, not here.

customers.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
customers.grain: One customer of one project — the demand-side counterpart of `suppliers`. The key is the customer's identifier AS THE SOURCE FILE SPELLS IT, scoped to the project, so the same company appearing in two projects is two rows and stays two rows.

governance.note: Adopted with RLS enabled and no `anon` policy. The logistics lanes carry an `*_anon_read` policy because the public network pages render them (D28, a standing decision); nothing reads this table at all, so there was no reader to keep working and no reason to widen that exposure. `audited: true` was NOT the first draft. The adoption was written with the three WP 2.3 triggers left off — the table had had no migration when they were written, so it had never had them — and `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` failed on the same commit that put the table in the contract. Its rule is derived from the contract's own tier, not from a list, so a tier-2 table without its triggers is a failure by construction. The triggers are in `20260916000003_adopt_customers_drop_product_code_map.sql` and R9 holds this field to them.

columns.meaning: The project this customer belongs to. Scoping is what makes `customer_id` a key: the same company in two projects is two rows, and merging them would merge two customers' models.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.meaning: The customer's identifier as the source file spells it. Joins to `outbound_logistics.customer_id`, which is the only place the identifier is used today — and the join is by string, untrimmed, which is D8's shape.

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: The customer's display name. Nullable; never a join key (G1).

columns.name: segment
columns.meaning: The customer's service segment, the axis the customer-echelon allocation policies tier on (`P-C.x`, blueprint §4.2 and Appendix A). NOT a closed vocabulary yet — there is no CHECK, because the policy that reads it does not exist, and inventing the set before the reader is how a column gets a constraint nobody can satisfy.
columns.note: DEFAULT 'default' is production's own default, adopted rather than chosen. It is a value, not an absence, and a later reader must not treat it as "unsegmented" without saying so at the point of display (§5 T2).

columns.name: priority_weight
columns.meaning: Relative allocation priority when demand exceeds supply. Dimensionless and relative — only the RATIO between two customers means anything, so a row at 1.0 is not "one unit" of anything.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine, and the blank is deliberate rather than unfinished. `scsim` has no customer-priority concept today: the customer echelon's allocation policies are `P-C.x` in the blueprint's catalog and none of them is implemented (§4.2, Appendix A). Whoever implements one traces this column then; wiring the mapper to a column the registry does not know is how a fallback ends up undeclared (I6).

columns.name: sla_fill_floor_pct
columns.meaning: The minimum fill rate the customer is contracted to receive, as a percentage. NULLABLE, and the null means "no contracted floor" — not zero. A reader that coerces it to 0 turns "unconstrained" into "no service required", which is D17's error in the other direction.
columns.note: NOT TRACED into the engine, for the same reason as `priority_weight`: the service-level policies that would read a contracted fill floor are `P-C.x` and none is implemented. Recorded here so the column is a declared gap rather than a silent one.

columns.meaning: When the row was last modified. Server-stamped.

columns.meaning: When the row was first inserted. Server-stamped.

customers.note: ADOPTED IN PHASE 3 / WP 3.0 (D43). This table existed in the production database with six rows and no creating migration, and it was invisible to the `no-orphan-table` gate for a reason worth keeping: R4 catches tables the CODE READS that no migration creates, and nothing has ever read this one. §15's schema probe — which keys on "production has it" rather than "the code reads it" — is what found it, and that probe now fails the verification run rather than reporting. NOTHING READS IT YET, and the sidecar says so in every `consumed_by: null`. It is not dead: its columns are the inputs of the customer-echelon policies (`P-C.x`), which is why it was adopted rather than dropped the way `product_code_map` was in the same migration. A later package gives it a writer, a CSV template and the tier-2 audit triggers; until then it is a described, governed, empty-of-readers table, which is a better state than an undescribed one holding the same six rows.

governance.note: Written by the `_build_dataset_snapshot` database function, never by a page — that is the INTENT, and `write: null` records it. **The enforcement does not match, and WP 2.4 measured it.** The live policy `dataset_versions_insert_all` is `FOR INSERT ... WITH CHECK (true)`, and `20260610000002` grants `anon` SELECT and INSERT, so any holder of the public anon key may insert a snapshot row. The contract reads narrower than the database, which is the exact class §9 asks this package to find. It is pinned by `governanceEnforcement.test.ts` rather than silently fixed: the app runs AS anon with no auth session, so revoking is a Phase 3 migration with an auth model behind it, and the decision taken was to document. delegation_grants.grain: One temporary, subtractive grant of project access from one person to another. `subtractive-delegation` (§2.1 G3) made real: a grant may never exceed what the grantor holds, and it always ends.

governance.note: `write: null` again literal. SELECT is limited to the grantor, the grantee and super admins; there is NO write policy, so RLS denies writes and `grant_project_delegation()` / `revoke_project_delegation()` are the only way in. That is forced rather than chosen: subtraction has to be CHECKED against the grantor's own level, and a PERMISSIVE policy cannot subtract (D28) — it can only add another OR'd way to say yes. `audited: false` is the uncomfortable one: a privilege grant that writes no audit row is exactly what `audit-actor` (§2.1 G4) exists to prevent, and WP 2.3 owns it. Recorded here rather than left to be noticed.

policies.name: delegation_grants: read own
policies.using: grantor_user_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR grantee_user_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR public.current_is_super_admin()
policies.with_check: grantor_user_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR grantee_user_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR public.current_is_super_admin()

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate identifier for the grant. What revoke takes.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project the grant applies to. A delegation is never org-wide.

columns.name: grantor_user_id
columns.meaning: Who gave it. Their effective project role at the moment of granting is the ceiling on what the grant may contain.

columns.name: grantee_user_id
columns.meaning: Who received it.

columns.name: project_role
columns.meaning: The level granted. Rejected by the RPC if it outranks the grantor's own — the subtractive rule, enforced in one place.

ingest.validate: one of owner / editor / analyst / viewer, and no higher than the grantor's own level

columns.name: expires_at
columns.meaning: When it stops granting. NOT NULL, and the RPC additionally refuses a time already past. A delegation without an end is a membership, and the product has a table for those.

columns.name: rationale
columns.meaning: Why the elevation exists. NOT NULL and non-empty, unlike on `project_members`: a temporary grant of someone else's access is exactly the thing a reviewer will later ask the reason for.

columns.name: revoked_at
columns.meaning: When it was withdrawn early, if it was. Revocation SETS this rather than deleting the row — who held what, and when, survives the withdrawal.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the grant was made. Server-stamped.

delegation_grants.note: Expiry and revocation are both applied inside `effective_project_role()` rather than by each caller, so "did you remember to check expires_at" is not a question any future reader has to answer. Verified against a live PostgreSQL in WP 2.2: a grant exceeding the grantor's level is rejected, one with no expiry is rejected, and a grant whose expiry passes stops granting (PLAN.md §16).

inbound_logistics.tier_name: canonical — the only tier humans edit
inbound_logistics.grain: One supply arc as the user uploaded it: this supplier can deliver this material to this plant, at this price and lead time, in this volume. NOT deduplicated — a second upload of the same row makes a second row (D5).

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all twelve sidecars change together.

policies.name: Inbound: modifiers only
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = inbound_logistics.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR ( SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1 ) = 'admin') )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = inbound_logistics.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) AND (p.modeler_id = public.get_current_user_id() OR ( SELECT user_role FROM public.get_current_approved_user() LIMIT 1 ) = 'admin') )

policies.name: Inbound: organization access
policies.using: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = inbound_logistics.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )
policies.with_check: EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM public.projects p WHERE p.id = inbound_logistics.project_id AND public.org_is_current_user_org(p.organization_id, p.organization) )

constraints.name: inbound_logistics_lead_time_unit_known
constraints.definition: CHECK (lead_time_unit IS NULL OR public.unit_days(lead_time_unit) IS NOT NULL)

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate row identifier. Carries no meaning and joins to nothing.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this arc belongs to. Every read is scoped by it.

engine.transform: filter, never read as a value

ingest.validate: set from the selected project, never from the CSV

columns.name: plant_name
columns.meaning: The focal plant receiving the material, by NAME. A displayable string used as a join key — the thing invariant G1 forbids; WP 2.1/3.3 replace it with a uuid.

ingest.validate: must equal the project's plant_name — a trigger raises otherwise

columns.name: supplier_id
columns.meaning: The supplier's code as the user's own systems spell it.

engine.transform: str(); no trimming (D8)

ingest.validate: non-empty after trim — NOT enforced today (D8)

columns.name: material_id
columns.meaning: The material's code as the user's own systems spell it. Joins to materials and the BOM.

engine.transform: str(); arcs whose material is not in the BOM are dropped

ingest.validate: non-empty after trim — NOT enforced today (D8)

columns.name: volume
columns.meaning: How much of this material the user buys from this supplier over one `time_unit`. A RATE, not a quantity — two rows are only comparable after both are converted to the same period.

engine.transform: rateToWeekly(volume, time_unit) — normalized to weeks

resolution.note: Volume is what the user's own systems recorded. It is not estimated; it is the thing other quantities are estimated FROM — demand_mean names it in estimable_from.

columns.name: time_unit
columns.meaning: The period `volume` is quoted over — day, week, month, quarter, year. It describes the VOLUME only. It says nothing about `lead_time`.

engine.transform: looked up in the one unit table

ingest.validate: one of day/week/month/quarter/year and their -ly spellings

resolution.note: A unit is never estimated. Unrecognised or blank is read on a 7-day basis, i.e. as already weekly (grading.ts::rateToWeekly).

columns.name: lead_time
columns.meaning: How long this supplier takes to deliver this material. The contract fixes the unit at WEEKS; `time_unit` does not apply to it and never has.

engine.transform: _duration_to_weeks(lead_time, lead_time_unit), then round and clamp to [1, 51]

substitutions.when: the column is NULL or zero
substitutions.visible_as: MappingWarning on the run's mapping report

resolution.note: The engine already supports this split and has since scsim was written: SupplierLink carries lead_time_weeks (the CENTRE) separately from lead_time_dist and lead_time_cv (the SPREAD), and core/engine.py samples only when the distribution is not DETERMINISTIC and the CV is above zero. So deterministic is not a degenerate case bolted on — it is the default path, and it skips sampling entirely. default_mode is `asserted` for the same reason: the user states the lead time, and the spread is opt-in. estimable_from names the observations tier that does not exist yet (tier 2-O, reserved in WP 1.2) rather than leaving the door open to estimating this from whatever happens to be lying around.

columns.note: Was `unit_source: fixed` until WP 1.3, and fixed by OMISSION rather than by contract: the engine read a `lead_time_unit` that no column supplied, so every lead time was taken as weeks whatever the user meant. The column now exists and `unit` stays `weeks` because that is what NULL still means.

engine_requirement.reason: Supplier lead time per sourcing arc — missing values default to 2 weeks.

columns.name: unit_price
columns.meaning: What one unit of this material costs from this supplier, delivered.

engine.transform: float(); a value <= 0 is replaced, not rejected

substitutions.visible_as: MappingWarning on the run's mapping report

substitutions.value: this arc's price becomes the material's cost, via the cheapest inbound arc
substitutions.visible_as: the effective-economics badge in /policies

resolution.note: hybrid is NULL because scsim has nowhere to put a spread: cost and unit_price are bare floats on Material and Product, with no distribution, no CV and no sampling path anywhere in the engine. Recording `hybrid: null` here is a statement about the ENGINE, not about the world — prices obviously vary. Giving them a spread is an engine change on the scsim track; see the RFC in PLAN.md §14. Do not invent one in this contract: a contract that describes a capability the engine does not have is how a fallback ends up in code with no contract entry, which is what I6 forbids in the other direction.

columns.note: The user types `unit_price` and the engine calls it `cost`. Both names are recorded because the manual must lead with the one the user typed (D21).

engine_requirement.reason: Purchase cost per sourcing arc — a missing price defaults to 1.0 and distorts procurement spend.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the row was inserted. Server-set.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row last changed. Server-set.

columns.name: lead_time_unit
columns.meaning: The period `lead_time` is quoted in — day, week, month, quarter or year. Blank means WEEKS, which is what the engine assumed before this column existed. Distinct from `time_unit`, which is the period `volume` is quoted over and has never applied to the lead time.

engine.transform: looked up in the one unit table; an unknown value falls to a 7-day basis

ingest.validate: one of the units public.unit_days() knows — enforced by the column's CHECK constraint

resolution.note: A unit is never estimated. NULL means weeks, matching project_map.py::_duration_to_weeks, and the column's CHECK constraint only admits units public.unit_days() knows.

columns.note: Added by WP 1.3 (D9). The engine had read this field since the scsim bridge was written; no column supplied it, so `r.get("lead_time_unit")` returned None on every row and a lead time entered in days was read as weeks — seven times too long, with no warning, because nothing in the chain knew a unit was expected. This is also the first use of the `contract` provenance state reserved in WP 1.2: the weeks default is supplied by this document, not guessed by code.

ingest_files.grain: One file as received, in one run: the manifest for bytes held in storage — where they are, how many there were, and the SHA-256 of exactly the sequence received. Write-once: the row records an event that has already happened and cannot be edited into a different one.

governance.note: RLS reaches the project through the run, the same predicate the staging tables use. The grant is narrower than theirs on purpose — `authenticated` holds SELECT and INSERT and nothing else — because tier 0 is write-once and a grant that permits UPDATE would be a promise the trigger then breaks. The trigger is the backstop the grant cannot be: the service role holds every privilege by definition, and `ingest_files_write_once()` refuses its updates too. `audited: false`, and here it is the most pointed of the four: a landing IS a tier transition, external bytes entering the system, and G4 says a tier transition writes an audit row naming the actor. What this table does instead is name the actor IN THE ROW (`uploaded_by`), which is better than nothing and less than the invariant asks. It has an owner: WP 3.2 writes the landing path, and an audit row is cheap to add from the function that already knows who uploaded the file — which is exactly the knowledge the service-role writers of D36 do not have.

policies.name: ingest_files: project access
policies.using: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM public.ingest_runs r WHERE r.id = ingest_files.ingest_run_id AND public.has_project_access(r.project_id))
policies.with_check: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM public.ingest_runs r WHERE r.id = ingest_files.ingest_run_id AND public.has_project_access(r.project_id))

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key for one landed file.

columns.name: ingest_run_id
columns.meaning: The run this file was landed for. NOT NULL: a file with no run is a byte-stream nobody asked for, and making the run the owner is what keeps a landing attached to a project, a source kind and an approval.
columns.note: ON DELETE CASCADE, and the direction matters: deleting a project deletes its runs and therefore its file manifests. Tier 0 is immutable, not immortal — a RESTRICT here would have made a project undeletable, which is a defect dressed as rigour.

columns.name: source_kind
columns.meaning: csv, orbit-mrp or api — what kind of source produced these bytes. The same closed vocabulary as the run's.
columns.note: No default here either, and unlike the other two tables this column never needed a backfill: the table is new and has no rows to be wrong about.

columns.name: original_filename
columns.meaning: The file's name as the user's machine gave it, verbatim. For display and for the person's own recognition — never a key, and never parsed for meaning: two projects upload `inbound.csv` on the same afternoon (G1's rule, applied to filenames).

columns.name: storage_bucket
columns.meaning: The storage bucket the bytes live in. Recorded rather than assumed, so that moving a bucket is a data change and not a code change.

columns.name: storage_path
columns.meaning: Where the bytes are inside the bucket. Generated by the writer, never supplied by the user, and UNIQUE with the bucket because it addresses exactly one stored object.

columns.name: content_type
columns.meaning: The MIME type as reported at upload. NULLABLE and not trusted: browsers report `application/vnd.ms-excel` for CSVs often enough that a parser keying on it would reject real files. WP 3.2's parser decides from the bytes.

columns.name: byte_size
columns.meaning: How many bytes were received. The cheapest possible check that a file is the file somebody meant to send, and the number a quota will eventually be about.

columns.name: content_sha256
columns.meaning: SHA-256 of the bytes AS RECEIVED, lowercase hex, computed before any parse. The anchor: with it, 'the file you uploaded on Tuesday' is a checkable claim rather than a memory.
columns.note: CHECK-constrained on SHAPE (`^[0-9a-f]{64}$`) rather than on content, because a truncated or upper-cased hash compares unequal to itself and would break every lineage claim built on it — quietly, and much later. It is also the dedup signal: 'you have uploaded these bytes before' is a question asked by hash, not by filename, and the index exists for it.

columns.name: uploaded_by
columns.meaning: The person who uploaded the file, in `approved_users`. NULL when the landing had no human — an API push or a scheduled pull — which is stated rather than filled with a service account.

columns.name: received_at
columns.meaning: When the bytes were received. Server-stamped, never the client's clock.

ingest_files.note: TIER 0, CREATED IN PHASE 3 / WP 3.1, AND NOTHING WRITES IT YET. PLAN.md §2 lists six tiers and this repository had five: there has never been a record of what a user actually uploaded. `UploadWizard` parses the file in the browser and throws it away, which is why every parse defect — D6's quoted comma, D7's blank numerics, D8's untrimmed identifiers, D46's integer `time_unit` — is unreproducible after the fact. You cannot re-read a file that was never kept. WP 3.2 is the writer: upload lands the bytes here, opens a run, and parses SERVER-SIDE. Landing the table one package ahead means that package does not have to invent a schema and a parser in the same session. WRITE-ONCE IS ENFORCED, NOT ASSERTED. `ingest_files_write_once()` refuses every UPDATE, and `supabase/rehearsal/060` proves it against a real database — both halves, because the rule is 'immutable' and not 'undeletable'. §2's tier laws have been sentences in a plan for three phases; a sentence nothing enforces drifts within two months, which is the lesson of the two orphan tables.

ingest_runs.grain: One ingestion attempt, from any source — a connector sync, a CSV upload or an API push — with the counts and the mapping report it produced. The unit a person reviews and approves: staged rows belong to a run, and promotion is a decision about a run rather than about a row.

governance.note: RLS keys on the run's own `project_id` — `has_project_access(project_id)` — which is WP 3.1's change. The original policy reached the project through `project_erp_links`, and a run with no link (`source_kind` csv or api) could not be reached that way at all: it would have been ungoverned rather than merely unsupported. `audited: false` is the honest record and it is a gap with an owner: the only writer today is the connector edge function running as the service role, which cannot name an actor (D36). WP 3.2 lands the upload path and is where the landing becomes an audited transition. `min_project_role: editor` states the intent — a viewer has no business opening an ingestion run — and nothing enforces the role yet; the policy is the modeler-or-admin predicate the connector shipped with.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. Not the grain: a run is identified by what it did, and nothing joins to this except the staging rows and the landed files.

columns.name: link_id
columns.meaning: The ERP link this run used, or NULL for a source that has none. NULL means 'this source needs no link', never 'the link was lost' — a CSV upload and an API push have no credential to point at.
columns.note: Was NOT NULL until WP 3.1. Nullable is the widening: with it, a run belongs to a project rather than to a connector.

columns.name: triggered_by
columns.meaning: manual or scheduled. A manual run was asked for by a person; a scheduled one was started by the cron sweep against the link's `sync_schedule_cron`.
columns.note: Not an engine input. It is the field that decides whether `triggered_by_user_id` is allowed to be NULL — a scheduled run has no person, and saying so is `audit-actor` (G4) being honest rather than inventing an actor.

columns.name: triggered_by_user_id
columns.meaning: The person who asked for a manual run, in `auth.users`. NULL for a scheduled run, where there is no person — stated rather than back-filled to a service account, because 'nobody asked, the schedule did' is the true answer (G4).

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: running, staged, applied, failed or skipped. `staged` is the state that matters: rows are in tier 1 and a human has not approved them. Nothing reaches tier 2 before `applied`.
columns.note: Not read by the engine and never will be: tier 1 is invisible below it (I2). The readers are the review UI and the connector's own auto-apply gate, which refuses to promote a run with any `fields_failed`.

columns.name: rows_fetched
columns.meaning: Row counts pulled from the source, per entity — {"products": 1007, "bom_versions": 25}. What the source OFFERED, which is not what was staged and not what was promoted.

columns.name: rows_new
columns.meaning: Staged rows the diff classified as new: no live row carries this source identifier yet.

columns.name: rows_changed
columns.meaning: Staged rows whose live counterpart exists and differs.

columns.name: rows_unchanged
columns.meaning: Staged rows identical to their live counterpart. Counted rather than dropped: 'nothing changed' is a result, and a report that omits it cannot be distinguished from one that failed.

columns.name: rows_removed
columns.meaning: Rows present in the live table under this source and absent from the pull — `diff_state = removed_upstream`. Never promoted by the connector: a source dropping a row is not authority to delete the project's row.

columns.name: mapping_warnings
columns.meaning: The per-field mapping report: [{level, entity, field, reason}], the same shape as `simulation_runs.mapping_warnings` and scsim's MappingWarning, so MappingWarningsCard renders it unmodified.

columns.name: fields_mapped
columns.meaning: Source fields that landed in a staged column with a value.

columns.name: fields_defaulted
columns.meaning: Source fields the source did not provide, left null for the project's defaults to fill at promotion. This is the count that drives the amber badge — a defaulted field is a substitution and §5 T2 says it is visible at the point of display.

columns.name: fields_failed
columns.meaning: Source fields that could not be mapped at all. A run with any failure never auto-applies, whatever the link's threshold says.

columns.name: diff_summary
columns.meaning: The rendered diff the review UI reads, kept until the run is applied or rejected. WP 3.4 builds that screen; the column is the connector's own and predates it.

columns.name: applied_at
columns.meaning: When the staged rows were promoted to tier 2. NULL for every run that has not been approved — which is most of them, by design.

columns.name: applied_by_user_id
columns.meaning: Who approved the promotion, in `auth.users`. NULL when the link's auto-apply threshold promoted it, and that NULL is the one D36 is about: an automatic promotion has no actor and says so rather than borrowing one.

columns.name: error_detail
columns.meaning: Why a failed run failed, in the source's own words. Kept verbatim: a paraphrased error is a second source for a fact that already had one.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the run opened. Server-stamped.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this run ingests into. Added in WP 3.1 and NOT NULL: it is what the RLS policy reads, so a run is governed by the project it writes to rather than by the credential it happened to use.
columns.note: Backfilled from `project_erp_links.project_id` for every row that existed. The backfill was total by construction — `link_id` was NOT NULL with a foreign key — which is why the migration sets NOT NULL without the guard `customers` needed.

columns.name: source_kind
columns.meaning: Where this run's rows came from: csv, orbit-mrp or api. CHECK-constrained, so a fourth source cannot appear without a migration that decides what it is.
columns.note: NO DEFAULT, deliberately. The column is backfilled to 'orbit-mrp' for the runs that existed and the default is then dropped, so the next writer must state its source. A default here would record a CSV upload as a connector sync and nobody would be told, which is the §5 T1 failure — a value with no provenance — inside the table that exists to record provenance.

ingest_runs.note: RENAMED FROM `erp_sync_runs` IN PHASE 3 / WP 3.1. The connector migration named it for the only source that existed and said in its own COMMENT ON TABLE that the name would be generalized in Phase 3; invariant `ingestion-contract` (I7) is why it had to be. A table whose name asserts one vendor cannot hold a second source's rows without lying about what it is. WHAT IS NOT HERE YET. Nothing writes a `csv` or `api` run: WP 3.2 builds the `ingest-file` edge function that does. The columns those runs need are here and described, which is the point of landing the schema one package ahead of its writer — WP 3.2 should not have to invent a schema and a parser in the same session. `supabase/rehearsal/050` and `060` assert what this table does: a connector run still stages, diffs and promotes identically, and a link-less run is legal and governed.

ingest_staged_bom_lines.grain: One component line of one staged BOM version, as the source sent it: this much of that component goes into one unit of the parent.

governance.note: RLS reaches the project through the RUN — `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ingest_runs r WHERE r.id = ingest_run_id AND has_project_access(r.project_id))`. WP 3.1 rewrote it: the original went through `project_erp_links`, which a run without a link cannot satisfy. Two things about this table were invisible to the contract until that rewrite, and both are worth recording. Its policy was created inside a `DO $$ EXECUTE format(...) $$` loop, which `introspect.mjs` does not read, so the contract recorded RLS enabled and ZERO policies and the generated page published that — D28's blind spot from the other side, hiding protection rather than exposure. The policies are now four literal statements. `audited: false`: no tier-2 transition happens here, and the writer is the service role (D36). The transition that DOES need an audit row is promotion, which WP 3.3 makes an audited upsert.

policies.name: ingest_staged_bom_lines: project access
policies.using: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM public.ingest_runs r WHERE r.id = ingest_staged_bom_lines.ingest_run_id AND public.has_project_access(r.project_id))
policies.with_check: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM public.ingest_runs r WHERE r.id = ingest_staged_bom_lines.ingest_run_id AND public.has_project_access(r.project_id))

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key for one staged row. The staging tables carry no natural key on purpose: they hold what a source SAID, including whatever duplicates it said it with, and deduplication is a decision made at promotion (WP 3.3), not a constraint that silently discards a source row before anybody has seen it.

columns.name: ingest_run_id
columns.meaning: The run that staged this row. The owner: staged rows cascade with their run, and the run is what carries the project, the source kind and the approval.
columns.note: Renamed from `sync_run_id` in WP 3.1, with the table it points at. WP 3.3 puts the same column on the tier-2 lanes, so one word covers the whole path from a file to a canonical row.

columns.name: link_id
columns.meaning: The ERP link the row came through, or NULL for a source that has none. Redundant with the run's own `link_id` and kept because the connector writes it; the RUN is the authority (I1) and a reader that disagrees should believe the run.

columns.name: external_id
columns.meaning: The row's identifier IN THE SOURCE, exactly as the source spells it. Never trimmed or case-folded here: tier 1 holds what arrived, and normalizing at this tier would destroy the evidence that a source sent `" MAT-1 "` (D8).

columns.name: external_bom_version_id
columns.meaning: The BOM header this line belongs to, in the source's identifier space — joins to `ingest_staged_bom_versions.external_id` within the run.

columns.name: external_component_product_id
columns.meaning: The component consumed, in the source's identifier space. Becomes the material side of a tier-2 BOM row once a promotion for BOMs exists.

columns.name: quantity_per_unit
columns.meaning: How much of the component one unit of the parent consumes, in the component's own unit of measure. The dimensionless-looking number that is not dimensionless: it is per unit of the PARENT, and the parent's unit is on the staged product.
columns.note: Untraced: nothing promotes BOM lines yet. `bom_single_level.consumption_rate` is the tier-2 column it becomes, and that column defaults to 1.0 when absent — a substitution the promotion will have to declare (I6) rather than apply quietly.

columns.name: scrap_factor
columns.meaning: The source's expected scrap on this line, as the source expresses it — a fraction in some systems and a percentage in others. NOT normalized here, and that ambiguity is the reason a promotion cannot simply copy it.
columns.note: Untraced, and deliberately not guessed. A 5 that means 5%% and a 0.05 that means the same thing differ by a factor of 100, and the engine has no scrap concept to receive either. Whoever promotes it names the source's convention first.

columns.name: raw
columns.meaning: The complete source row, verbatim. The reason a field the mapper does not yet understand is not lost: when a column turns out to matter, the answer for rows already staged is in here rather than in a re-sync.

columns.name: diff_state
columns.meaning: new, changed, unchanged or removed_upstream — what the sync decided this row is, relative to the live tier-2 table. `removed_upstream` is the one with teeth: it is NEVER promoted, because a source dropping a row is not authority to delete the project's row.
columns.note: Computed by the connector as a full-refresh comparison against `products.source_external_id`. WP 3.4 renders it and WP 3.3 makes promotion an upsert keyed on the natural key, at which point `changed` and `new` stop being a guess about what the upsert will do.

columns.name: staged_at
columns.meaning: When the row landed in staging. Server-stamped, and it is what the promotion copies into `products.source_synced_at`, so a live row can say how old the source data behind it is.
columns.note: Renamed from `synced_at` in WP 3.1: a CSV upload is not a sync, and the column had to mean the same thing for every source kind or it would have needed a second one.

columns.name: source_kind
columns.meaning: csv, orbit-mrp or api — where this row came from. CHECK-constrained, and it matches its run's value for every row any current writer produces.
columns.note: NO DEFAULT after the backfill: a writer states its source. Duplicated from the run deliberately — a staged row is read in bulk and joining to the run to learn what it is would make the common read the expensive one. If the two ever disagree the run wins.

columns.name: fact_class
columns.meaning: master or transactional. Master rows describe things that persist — an item, a BOM, a supplier; transactional rows describe events with a date. Nothing stages transactional rows yet; the vocabulary exists so WP 3.2's parser has one to declare against rather than inventing one per file.

materials.grain: One material in one project: the economics the simulation reads for it. The precision path — the CSV lanes carry prices too, and where this row is silent the engine derives the value from them rather than treating it as missing.

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all thirteen sidecars change together. SEPARATELY — AND THIS REPLACES WHAT WP 1.2 WROTE HERE, WHICH WAS WRONG: this sidecar used to assert `rls_enabled: false` and say "no migration ever runs ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on them". One does. `20260614000001_item_master.sql:57-66` enables RLS and creates two policies (`%s_auth_all`, `%s_anon_read`) on each of the three masters — but through `EXECUTE format(...)` inside a `FOREACH` over an array of table names, which a static replay of the migrations cannot evaluate. The introspector recorded the absence as `enabled: false`, WP 1.2 read that as fact, and the contract was one generated page away from telling a user their item masters were unprotected. WP 1.4 fixed the mechanism, not the guess: the introspector now records dynamic DDL (`dynamic_ddl`) and marks the tables it touches `rls.determinate: false`, the validator refuses to let a sidecar assert an RLS state the migrations do not settle, and the generated page says the state is indeterminate and names the migration. The ONLY way to know is to read the live database — PLAN.md §15, still unrun. WP 2.4's security review owns it.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The project this material belongs to. Half of the primary key.

engine.transform: filter, never read as a value

ingest.validate: set from the selected project, never from the CSV

columns.name: material_id
columns.meaning: The material's code as the user's own systems spell it. Joins to the BOM and to every inbound arc that supplies it.

engine.transform: str()

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: A human-readable name for the material. Display only.

engine.transform: str(name or material_id)

resolution.note: A label. Recorded for completeness: every engine-consumed field carries a resolution block, including the ones where the answer is trivial.

columns.name: cost
columns.meaning: What one unit of this material costs to buy. The master value; where it is unset the engine uses the cheapest inbound arc instead, which is usually what the user wants and is why leaving it blank is not an error.

engine.transform: float() when > 0
engine.missing_default: the cheapest inbound unit_price for this material, floored at 1.0

substitutions.value: the cheapest inbound arc's unit_price (grading.ts::cheapestInboundCost floors a <= 0 price to 1.0 first)
substitutions.visible_as: the effective-economics badge in /policies

resolution.note: hybrid is NULL because scsim has nowhere to put a spread: cost and unit_price are bare floats on Material and Product, with no distribution, no CV and no sampling path anywhere in the engine. Recording `hybrid: null` here is a statement about the ENGINE, not about the world — prices obviously vary. Giving them a spread is an engine change on the scsim track; see the RFC in PLAN.md §14. Do not invent one in this contract: a contract that describes a capability the engine does not have is how a fallback ends up in code with no contract entry, which is what I6 forbids in the other direction. estimable_from is empty for a second reason: the value already has a derivation — the cheapest inbound arc — and that is a substitution the user can see and trace, not an estimate.

engine_requirement.reason: Inventory valuation and holding cost — the terminal default of 1.0 makes every cost KPI meaningless.
engine_requirement.fallback: cheapest inbound unit_price across the material's suppliers

columns.name: holding_cost_pct
columns.unit: fraction of unit value per year
columns.meaning: The annual cost of holding one unit in stock, as a fraction of its value. 0.2 means holding a unit for a year costs a fifth of what the unit is worth.

engine.transform: falls back to the inventory policy bundle's holding_cost_pct when NULL
engine.missing_default: the project's inventory policy bundle value (0.2 in the shipped default)

substitutions.visible_as: the policy grid's provenance dot

resolution.note: A financial policy parameter, not an observation: it is what the business decides holding stock costs it. Falls back to the project's inventory bundle, which is a policy default and is visible as one.

columns.name: moq
columns.meaning: Minimum order quantity: the smallest amount this material can be ordered in. A commercial fact the supplier states, not something to be inferred from order history.

engine.transform: float(moq) when truthy, else 0.0 — applied per (supplier, material) link

resolution.note: estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. Fitting a distribution to it would produce a number with error bars around something that has no error, and the error bars would be believed. A future estimator reading this contract must refuse this field. A minimum order quantity is a term the supplier states. Inferring it from observed order sizes learns the ordering policy, not the constraint — and then the simulation optimises against its own past behaviour.

columns.name: initial_on_hand
columns.meaning: How much of this material is in stock when the simulation starts.

engine.transform: float() when not None; None is passed through as None, not as zero

resolution.note: Opening stock is a measurement — someone counted it — so it is the one master economic field where an observations tier could legitimately supply it. Nothing does today.

columns.name: lead_time_dist
columns.meaning: The SHAPE of this material's delivery lead time — deterministic, or a named distribution around the arc's lead time. `deterministic` means the lead time is exactly what the arc says, every time.

engine.transform: LeadTimeDist(value) when set, else LeadTimeDist.DETERMINISTIC

ingest.validate: one of the LeadTimeDist enum values; `empirical` is reserved for the data-import path (M7) and is not selectable yet

resolution.note: The SPREAD half of lead_time's hybrid; the centre is inbound_logistics.lead_time. LeadTimeDist.EMPIRICAL exists in the enum and is RESERVED for the data-import path (M7) — it is the value an estimator would write, which is why it is not offered in the UI today. `deterministic` is the default and means the lead time is exactly what the arc says.

columns.name: lead_time_cv
columns.meaning: How much the lead time varies, as a coefficient of variation. Read only when `lead_time_dist` is not deterministic: the engine skips sampling entirely when the distribution is deterministic or the CV is zero.

engine.transform: float() when truthy, else 0.0

resolution.note: The magnitude of lead_time's spread. Read only when lead_time_dist is not deterministic: core/engine.py tests both, so a CV on a deterministic link is silently inert. Zero and NULL are the same thing here.

governance.note: A member may read only their OWN membership row (`user_id = get_current_user_id()`); there is no policy letting a member enumerate who else is in their organization, and the admin pages that do so run through super-admin RPCs. `audited: false` is the honest record — `admin_add_org_member` and friends log through `log_admin_action`, but membership rows are also written by the `20260709000002` backfill and by nothing else that audits, so the general claim fails. columns.meaning: Surrogate row identifier. The membership's identity is (org_id, user_id).

columns.name: org_id
columns.meaning: The organization joined, by uuid. ON DELETE CASCADE — deleting a tenant removes its memberships rather than orphaning them.

columns.name: user_id
columns.meaning: The approved user who is a member, by uuid. ON DELETE CASCADE.

columns.name: org_role
columns.meaning: The member's standing in the organization — `owner`, `admin` or `member`, CHECK-constrained. This is an ORG vocabulary and it is not the project vocabulary: `min_project_role` throughout this contract speaks of viewer / analyst / editor / owner, which WP 2.2 creates on `project_members`. The two share the word "owner" and mean different things by it.

substitutions.when: a member row is inserted without a role
substitutions.visible_as: the column default, and the admin member list renders the resulting role verbatim

columns.note: NOT READ BY THE ACCESS LAYER TODAY. `capabilities_for_user()` resolves role -> org -> user through `approved_users.role` and the capability tables; no policy and no RPC consults `org_role`. An organization `admin` therefore holds no more than a `member` does, which is the gap WP 2.2 closes when it extends the resolver. Recorded rather than implied, per §5 T1.

columns.meaning: When the membership was created. Server-stamped.

organizations.grain: One tenant. Every project, every dataset and every simulation result in the product belongs to exactly one of these rows, and the boundary between two of them is the boundary the whole access layer is built to hold.

governance.note: `write: super_admin` is enforced, not aspirational: every mutation goes through `admin_create_organization` / `admin_update_organization` / `admin_set_org_status`, each of which opens with `_assert_super_admin` and closes with `log_admin_action`. This is one of the few tables where `audited: true` is literally true today — WP 2.3 is what makes the claim general. Read is open to any member of the org via the self-bridge policy below, which WP 2.1 rewrote: it matched the caller's TEXT org against `name` or `slug`, so renaming an organization revoked its own members' read on the row that had just been renamed. It now bridges on `id` first.

policies.name: orgs: members read own
policies.using: id = public.get_current_user_org_id(public.get_current_user_id()) OR name = public.get_current_user_org() OR slug = public.get_current_user_org()

columns.meaning: The organization's identity. This is the value that must travel — it is what `projects.organization_id`, `approved_users.organization_id` and the public /v1 API's `p_org_id` all mean. Not displayable, and that is the property that makes it safe as a join key (§2.1 `uuid-identity`).

columns.name: name
columns.meaning: The organization's display name, as an administrator typed it. EDITABLE and NOT UNIQUE — two organizations may legitimately share one. It is a label for humans and it is never an identity.
columns.note: D13's join key. `admin_update_organization` updates this column and nothing else: no trigger, no cascade, and no second UPDATE reaching `approved_users.organization` or `projects.organization`. So a rename leaves those two text copies holding the OLD string, and the next user approved into the organization carries the NEW one — at which point a text comparison between them can never match again. WP 2.1 routes every such comparison through `org_is_current_user_org(uuid, text)`.

columns.name: slug
columns.meaning: A URL-safe form of the name, `lower(regexp_replace(name, '[^a-zA-Z0-9]+', '-', 'g'))` at the moment the row was seeded. UNIQUE, and deliberately NOT recomputed on rename — so after a rename it is a record of what the organization used to be called, which is what makes it usable to match rows written before it.

columns.name: owner_user_id
columns.meaning: The approved user who owns the tenant. Advisory today — nothing in RLS or any RPC reads it; ownership is expressed through `organization_members.org_role = 'owner'`. Two places holding the same fact is an I1 violation waiting to diverge; WP 2.2 owns the resolution.

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: Whether the tenant is live — `active` or `suspended`, CHECK-constrained to those two. Set through `admin_set_org_status`.
columns.note: SUSPENSION IS NOT ENFORCED IN THE DATA LAYER. No policy and no RPC consults this column before granting access — a suspended organization's members read and write exactly as before. It is a label the admin pages render. Recorded here rather than left to be discovered, per §5 T1; the enforcement belongs with WP 2.2's resolver, which is where a capability decision is made once instead of inevery policy.

columns.name: settings
columns.meaning: Per-tenant configuration, free-form. No key of it is read by any migration, edge function or page today; it is a forward-declared extension point.

columns.name: created_at
columns.meaning: When the organization was created. Server-stamped.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.meaning: When the row was last modified. Server-stamped by DEFAULT only — no trigger maintains it, and `admin_update_organization` does not set it, so a renamed organization still shows its creation time here.

organizations.note: Created by `20260709000002_super_admin_phase1.sql`, which seeded one row per DISTINCT `approved_users.organization` string. That seeding is why the uuid plane and the text plane started out agreeing, and why nothing has kept them agreeing since: the seed ran once, `set_project_defaults()` never stamped the uuid (D27), and `admin_update_organization` renames without propagating. WP 2.1 fixed the trigger, backfilled what it could match unambiguously, and routed every live comparison through one predicate. It deliberately did NOT re-seed this table from distinct strings: after a rename, a user carrying the new name slugifies to a slug no row holds, and seeding would split one organization into two.

outbound_logistics.grain: One demand arc as the user uploaded it: this customer buys this product from this plant, at this price and lead time, in this volume. NOT deduplicated — a second upload of the same row makes a second row (D5).

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all twelve sidecars change together.

governance.note: `write` names the capability that exists today. WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all thirteen sidecars change together. SEPARATELY — AND THIS REPLACES WHAT WP 1.2 WROTE HERE, WHICH WAS WRONG: this sidecar used to assert `rls_enabled: false` and say "no migration ever runs ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on them". One does. `20260614000001_item_master.sql:57-66` enables RLS and creates two policies (`%s_auth_all`, `%s_anon_read`) on each of the three masters — but through `EXECUTE format(...)` inside a `FOREACH` over an array of table names, which a static replay of the migrations cannot evaluate. The introspector recorded the absence as `enabled: false`, WP 1.2 read that as fact, and the contract was one generated page away from telling a user their item masters were unprotected. WP 1.4 fixed the mechanism, not the guess: the introspector now records dynamic DDL (`dynamic_ddl`) and marks the tables it touches `rls.determinate: false`, the validator refuses to let a sidecar assert an RLS state the migrations do not settle, and the generated page says the state is indeterminate and names the migration. The ONLY way to know is to read the live database — PLAN.md §15, still unrun. WP 2.4's security review owns it.

columns.name: production_capacity
columns.meaning: How much of this product the plant can make per week. The canonical G4 example: when it is unset the engine invents a capacity generous enough that capacity never binds, so an unset value silently turns off the constraint the user thinks they are simulating.

engine.transform: float() when > 0
engine.missing_default: max(2 x demand, 1000) — a value chosen so the constraint never binds

substitutions.visible_as: MappingWarning on the run's mapping report

resolution.note: estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. Fitting a distribution to it would produce a number with error bars around something that has no error, and the error bars would be believed. A future estimator reading this contract must refuse this field. This is the canonical G4 field: unset, the engine invents max(2 x demand, 1000), which is chosen so the constraint never binds. Estimating it from output would do the same thing with more ceremony — output is bounded by demand, so the fitted capacity can never explain a shortage.

engine_requirement.reason: With no capacity source the engine defaults to max(2·demand, 1000), so plant capacity never binds.

project_erp_links.grain: One authorized link between one project and one company in one external system: project ownership proved on this side, company membership proved on that side by the linking user's own OAuth consent. One link is one credential and one project — never shared, so revoking one project's link cannot be bypassed by a sibling.

governance.note: One FOR ALL policy — `has_project_access(project_id)` — so reading and writing a link are the same permission: whoever can administer the project can connect it to a source and disconnect it. That is deliberate and it is also the loosest thing on this page, because `min_project_role: owner` is the intent and nothing enforces a project role yet (WP 2.2 landed the resolver; no policy here calls it). `audited: false` is the one that should be uncomfortable: creating a link grants an external system standing access to a project's data and revoking one takes it away, and neither writes an audit row. It is not a tier transition, so G4 does not formally cover it; it is a governance event by any reading of §5, and it is recorded here as a named gap rather than left to be noticed. The table's own honesty is elsewhere and it is real: `status`, `status_detail`, `last_verified_at` and `revoked_at` mean a revoked link says when and why. NO `rls_enabled` FIELD, and its absence is the point. The connector migration enables RLS on this table in a plain statement and creates its policy in another — but the same file also builds the staging policies inside a `DO $$ EXECUTE format(...) $$` loop whose SQL mentions this table, so the introspector marks its RLS indeterminate: "the migrations do not say", which is a different claim from "off" and may not be rendered as one. Only the live database can answer (§15), and a sidecar may not assert what the schema does not settle.

columns.name: id
columns.meaning: Surrogate key. The link's identity for every run that used it.

columns.name: project_id
columns.meaning: The SuReSuite project this link feeds. One side of the two-sided grant.

columns.name: external_system
columns.meaning: Which external system — `orbit-mrp` is the only value any code writes. Free text, not CHECK-constrained, and that is the one place this table still assumes a single vendor: `ingest_runs.source_kind` is the closed vocabulary WP 3.1 added, and it is the one a reader should trust.
columns.note: A second connector would add a value here AND a `source_kind`, and the two would have to agree. Whoever adds it: make this column a CHECK, or derive it. Two vocabularies for one fact is what I1 exists to prevent, and this is the half WP 3.1 did not close.

columns.name: external_company_id
columns.meaning: The company/tenant identifier IN THE EXTERNAL SYSTEM. Part of the natural key with the project and the system: one project may link one company of one system exactly once.

columns.name: external_company_name
columns.meaning: The company's display name, cached for the picker and refreshed on each sync. A LABEL and never a key (G1) — the id above is what the grant is about.

columns.name: linked_by_user_id
columns.meaning: The person whose own OAuth consent proved membership of that company, in `auth.users`. NOT NULL because the link IS that proof: there is no way to create one from a hand-typed company id, and an unattributed link would be a credential with no owner.

columns.name: external_oauth_token_ref
columns.meaning: The NAME of a secret in Supabase Vault, never a token. `get_erp_oauth_token(p_ref)` resolves it and is granted to `service_role` only, so a browser session cannot read the credential even though it can read this row.
columns.note: The pointer is readable by any project member and the value is not. That is the design: a per-link, per-user delegated token, so revoking one project's link cannot be bypassed by a sibling project.

columns.name: status
columns.meaning: active, needs_attention or revoked. A sync re-verifies both sides before touching data and revokes the link on failure rather than continuing on the old assumption.
columns.note: Not an engine input. It is the field the sync path reads first, and `revoked` is terminal: the connector never resurrects a link, a person re-links.

columns.name: status_detail
columns.meaning: Why the status is what it is, in words a user can act on — "Access revoked in orbit-mrp — reconnect". The reason a revoked link is not a mystery.

columns.name: last_verified_at

When a second connector arrives, the question to ask is whether it shares this shape (a per-user delegated token proving membership of an external tenant) or needs its own; `ingest_runs.source_kind` already carries the distinction that matters to everything downstream. projects.grain: One modelling project: a named supply chain, owned by one modeller, belonging to one organization. It is the SCOPE, and its access rules are the ones every other table inherits by joining to it — which is why WP 2.1 had to redefine 58 policies on 24 other tables to change one comparison. Read is org-wide (any member of the owning organization sees every project in it); write is restricted to the project's own modeller or a global `admin`. risk_data.note: The second of WP 1.4's three orphans (D4), and the one that turned out not to be an orphan at all. Two network pages read it and no migration created it — but the table EXISTS in the production database, untracked, with the spreadsheet-header columns `COUNTRY` and `"RISK CLASS"`. CI proved it: the first version of the migration was a plain `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, which no-opped, and the next statement failed on a column that was not there. Same class as `approved_users`: created outside migration tracking, invisible to a static replay, which can only tell you no migration creates a table and not whether one exists. `20260915000003_risk_data.sql` now both builds it on a fresh database and ADOPTS the one already there — renaming the quoted columns, adding the provenance columns, and marking the pre-contract rows `source: 'unrecorded (loaded before the reference-tier contract)'` rather than inventing a publisher for them. The new CHECKs land `NOT VALID` on the adopted table: enforced for every future write, not retroactively asserted about rows nobody has looked at.

WP 2.2 splits `data_editing` into `data_edit_inputs` (tier 2) and `data_edit_policies` (tier 4); this row becomes `data_edit_inputs` then, and all thirteen sidecars change together. SEPARATELY — AND THIS REPLACES WHAT WP 1.2 WROTE HERE, WHICH WAS WRONG: this sidecar used to assert `rls_enabled: false` and say "no migration ever runs ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on them". One does. `20260614000001_item_master.sql:57-66` enables RLS and creates two policies (`%s_auth_all`, `%s_anon_read`) on each of the three masters — but through `EXECUTE format(...)` inside a `FOREACH` over an array of table names, which a static replay of the migrations cannot evaluate. The introspector recorded the absence as `enabled: false`, WP 1.2 read that as fact, and the contract was one generated page away from telling a user their item masters were unprotected. WP 1.4 fixed the mechanism, not the guess: the introspector now records dynamic DDL (`dynamic_ddl`) and marks the tables it touches `rls.determinate: false`, the validator refuses to let a sidecar assert an RLS state the migrations do not settle, and the generated page says the state is indeterminate and names the migration. The ONLY way to know is to read the live database — PLAN.md §15, still unrun. WP 2.4's security review owns it.

resolution.note: estimable_from is EMPTY and that is a positive statement, not an omission. This is an engineering or commercial fact that someone knows exactly — it is written on a drawing, in a contract, or on a machine's nameplate. Fitting a distribution to it would produce a number with error bars around something that has no error, and the error bars would be believed. A future estimator reading this contract must refuse this field. Capacity is what the supplier CAN ship, not what they HAVE shipped. Estimating it from delivery history caps it at observed demand, so a capacity constraint fitted this way can never bind and can never explain a shortage — which is precisely the question it exists to answer. columns.name: plant_name
columns.meaning: The focal plant this edge belongs to, by NAME — the join key G1 forbids. Renamed from `plant` by 20250822025432, which is also when its incorrect UNIQUE constraint stopped meaning one-row-per-plant.

engine.transform: copied from the lane row

columns.name: weighted
columns.meaning: The volume on this edge after unit normalization — always per WEEK, whatever period the uploaded row quoted. This is where D2's fix lands: before it, a supplier quoting 52 000 a year and one quoting 1 000 a week were summed as 52 000 and 1 000.

engine.consumed_by: the analyzers and the policy grid's volume basis; not the engine mapping
engine.transform: weeklyVolume(volume, time_unit) in _shared/laneVolumes.ts, over grading.ts's one unit table

columns.note: numeric(16,6) since 20250816031317. Normalization SHRINKS every value quoted coarser than a day and multiplies day-quoted rows by 7, so overflow needs a pre-existing value above ~1.43e9 in a day-quoted project. Bounded by analysis, not measurement — the §15 baseline has never been run.

columns.name: material_consumption_rate
columns.unit: units of upstream per unit of downstream
columns.meaning: How much of the upstream item one unit of the downstream item consumes, carried through from the BOM.

engine.consumed_by: the analyzers and the network pages; not the engine mapping
engine.transform: copied from bom consumption_rate, multiplied down multi-level chains

columns.name: sourcing_ratio
columns.unit: fraction of the destination's inbound flow
columns.meaning: This edge's share of everything flowing into its destination. A share, so the D2 unit error did not cancel: it decides which supplier the platform calls primary.

engine.consumed_by: the policy grid's primary-source suggestion; the analyzers
engine.transform: volumeShare(weeklyVolume(row), weeklyVolumeTotalsBy(...)) in _shared/laneVolumes.ts

supply_chain_data_multi_tier.tier_name: derived — a pure function of tier 2
supply_chain_data_multi_tier.grain: One edge of the DEEP supply graph — tier-2 and tier-3 suppliers behind the direct ones. Computed by the same ETL, read by the network pages, and NOT propagated into the simulation: the engine models a single focal plant with three echelons (blueprint §2.4).

governance.note: Written by the `combine-project` edge function, never by a page. Invariant I2: pages never write tier 3. `write: null` is therefore a statement, not an omission — there is no user-facing write path and there must not be one. For precision, since WP 2.4 checked it: three PROJECT-SCOPED write policies do exist here, serving that ETL path. They are consistent with `write: null`, which names the capability gating a USER-facing write and not the existence of any policy — and unlike `dataset_versions` they carry a real predicate, so they do not admit an arbitrary holder of the table grant.
